newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia rebels to free captive troops in one group.
newsitem.headline: Colombia rebels to free captive troops in one group.

text.p: Colombia's largest guerrilla army said on Sunday it would release in a single group 60 soldiers it took prisoner almost nine months ago, but said the handover would not be within the "next few days."
An international spokesman for the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), set up as a pro-Soviet force in 1964, said 10 marines captured in January would also be freed at the same time.
The comments, in a phone interview with Reuters, come after a week of intense local media speculation that the rebels were about to begin handing over the soldiers in small groups.

The 60 soldiers were seized when the FARC overran a jungle base in Colombia's southern jungles on Aug. 30 signalling the start of Latin America's longest-running hostage crisis, which was recently overshadowed by the siege of the Japanese embassy residence in Lima.
The attack, in which 27 other soldiers died, marked the start of one of the bloodiest rebel offensives in more than three decades of Colombia's guerrilla uprising.

"The soldiers will not be handed over tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. The FARC ratifies its position that until the zone of southern Caqueta province is demilitarized the prisoners of war will not be freed," a FARC spokesman said.
"We will be handing over not only the 60 soldiers but also the 10 marines all at once. It's false that we will be handing them over in small groups," he added.
Last Wednesday the Radionet radio network claimed to have interviewed one of the captive soldiers and said a first group, of about 15 soldiers, would be released the next day.
The claims proved unfounded and the FARC spokesman said no journalists had so far been allowed to interview soldiers.

"The interview was not a real interview with one of our prisoners of war ... We think this was set up by military intelligence to create false expectations among the media and the families of the soldiers," the spokesman said.
The FARC has insisted that the army withdraws from a huge swathe of Caqueta for 10 days to two weeks before it will release its captives.
President Ernesto Samper ordered the demilitarization of part of the province last December, but the FARC declined to free its prisoners, calling for further concessions.

In an interview with the weekly political magazine Semana on Sunday, Jose Noe Rios, the government representative in charge of negotiating the soldiers' release, admitted the prisoners were unlikely to be released for "at least two weeks".
